title: Eat, drink, don't waste
hookLine: eat and drink but don't be wasteful (7:31)
last: LIBAS — THE BEST CLOTHING IS INSIDE.

cards: Open almost any fridge on a Sunday night. Half a bag of spinach gone slimy. The rice nobody wanted.

A yogurt two weeks past its date. Food that was paid for goes in the bin, and more gets bought. At the other end of the scale, a hadith shows the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ washing for prayer with about a double handful of water.
Between those two pictures sits a short line in surah seven that sounds almost too simple to need saying.

teach.b: In Pickthall's words: “O Children of Adam! Look to your adornment at every place of worship, and eat and drink, but be not prodigal. Lo! He loveth not the prodigals.” Two halves. The first is about clothing again.

A report in Sahih Muslim explains why: before Islam, some people circled the Ka'bah unclothed, and this verse told them to come to worship dressed, even dressed well. The second half is about the table. Eat.
Drink. Enjoy it; the next verse asks who could forbid the good things Allah has provided. But don't commit israf.
The root s-r-f means to go past the limit, to overshoot: israf is excess, beyond what's needed.
The Qur'an has a separate word, tabdhir, in surah seventeen, for scattering wealth away on nothing, and it's sharp about both.

teach.h: A THIRD, A THIRD, A THIRD.
teach.b: A hadith in Tirmidhi gives a measure for eating: a third of the stomach for food, a third for drink, a third for breath.

And Bukhari records that the Prophet made wudu with a mudd, roughly what two cupped hands hold, and bathed with only a few times that. Teachers take it as a lesson: enough is a real amount, and you can find it.
The verse doesn't say eat less than you need, or never enjoy food. It says eat, drink, and stop at enough. The opposite of israf isn't hunger.
It's the right amount, used well.

how: Muslims are taught to avoid israf in food, water and money; some keep the hadith of thirds in mind at meals, and teachers often point to the small amount of water the Prophet used for wudu.

o: excess: going past the limit, beyond need
eating any food that isn't lawful
fasting for longer than the law requires

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: the water for the Prophet's wudu

s: 7:31 tells people not to enjoy food
it says eat and drink, and the next verse defends the good things provided. it forbids excess.
the first half of 7:31 is about dressing for worship
Muslim's collection says some once circled the Ka'bah unclothed.
Bukhari records the Prophet making wudu with about two handfuls of water
a mudd, roughly what two cupped hands can hold.

games.q: you're at a big family dinner, still hungry for a second plate. what does the hadith of thirds suggest?
o: eat, but leave a third for drink and a third for breath.
games.why: a third for food, a third for drink, a third for breath (Tirmidhi). enough is the goal, not hunger.

practice: Walk through the day ahead in your mind and look, without judging, for the leaks: water running while you brush your teeth, food that will go bad, a light on in an empty room, a purchase you don't need.
Then picture your next meal, eaten slowly, ending at enough, with a little room left for breath.

wordCard.voice: Israf. Excess, going past the limit. Surah seven: eat and drink, but don't be wasteful, for Allah does not love the wasteful. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: excess, extravagance, from s-r-f, to go past the limit.

carryVoice: Your line: enough, no waste. The good things are a gift to enjoy. Day four hundred seven.
